purpose: Explicit native source selections compared by stanza content. Rockhill index entries are discovery references; native chapter and pāda spans are independently selected. The opening and ending anchors pin the checked passage.

selections.note: The published index points to the neighboring world-as-foam variant. Derge also has a closer body-as-foam stanza, selected here.
The Tibetan wording includes a negative in the line on the good person's fragrance going upwind, followed by diffusion in all directions.
Monthly grass-tip eating and the one-sixteenth comparison are shared. The Tibetan comparison is with faith in the true Dharma.
The Tibetan image is of washers using water and fletchers using fire.
The Tibetan bird-trace stanza has a different opening and names exhaustion of the taints but does not mention nonattachment to food.
Derge names sickness and old age driving people into the presence of the lord of death.
The Tibetan list has a different arrangement of the bodily and mental afflictions.
Derge ends with a question about discarding this old, diseased body.
Derge retains scattered bones and the question of delight but omits the autumn-gourd image.
Derge speaks to the house-builder and retains recurring births and suffering, with no explicit search clause.
Derge retains the house-builder and the broken beams but omits the closing clause about exhaustion of craving.
Derge ends with people lying curled up and recalling what they did before, without the spent-arrow simile.
Derge has the decorated royal chariot image but asks one to look at the body rather than the world.
Tibetan has the sun and moon free of clouds.
Tibetan retains the shining sun and moon image but applies it to youthful going forth into the Buddha's teaching.
The Tibetan stanza combines the refuge and four-truths verses, with the eightfold path in the same stanza. The shared stanza is displayed once, at 190.
Derge adds the happiness of meeting the steadfast as of meeting kin.
Tibetan describes living without harm among those who harm.
The Tibetan characterization names ethical conduct, conscience, and truthful speech.
The Tibetan stanza combines making an island with a smith and silver image also associated with the next Pāli position.
Derge distributes the giving and envy clauses across two neighboring stanzas. The first opens with welcoming a wise renunciant.
Tibetan illustrates severance with cutting the top of a palm tree.
Tibetan uses mire for desire and harm for hatred, retaining the net and river images for delusion and craving.
The Tibetan comparison includes the dice cheat concealing a throw.
Tibetan describes one who has left good and evil and practices the holy life, with a different list of qualities.
The longer Tibetan stanza adds a repeated opening about shaving one's head.
Tibetan shares the instruction to do the work oneself and the Tathāgata's role as teacher. Its first two lines resemble the preceding Pāli verse and it omits the meditators' release clause.
Derge has neighboring stanzas on emptiness and not-self. The not-self stanza refers specifically to formations.
Derge uses a badly grasped arrow in place of kusa grass.
The Tibetan verse retains the guarded frontier city and the instruction not to waste the opportunity, without the hell conclusion.
The shame contrast is the first two lines of a six-line native stanza. The next Pāli position uses the final four lines of that same stanza.
The danger and wrong-view contrast forms the concluding four lines of the six-line stanza that begins with the shame contrast.
Tibetan describes the monk who delights in heedfulness and sees danger in heedlessness, then retains the image of an elephant escaping a bog.
Tibetan uses the king and the forsaken kingdom, and adds the instruction to do no evil when walking alone.
Tibetan celebrates delight in meaningful speech in the line corresponding to the acquisition of wisdom.
The Tibetan wording shares the monkey seeking fruit and repeated wandering, without the opening creeper simile.
Derge preserves uprooting craving like grass dug up for its roots but does not add the final river and reed image.
Tibetan preserves the thirty-six streams image and connects their flow with the stream of mind.
The Tibetan wording retains the forest, renewed bondage, and invitation to look.
Tibetan describes a monk who receives only enough for himself and delights the gods. It omits the comparison to monks with more offerings.
The Tibetan no-ownership stanza refers to having no stores and not grieving over what is absent.
The concentration and wisdom pair is retained. Derge concludes by calling a person who has both a monk.
The insight into the aggregates' arising and passing and the joy it brings are shared. Derge omits the deathless conclusion.
Derge adds an opening on cultivation of concentration and wisdom before the restraint and contentment instructions.
The Tibetan verse covers choosing companions, sharing, and conduct. It has no closing joy and end-of-suffering couplet here.
The Tibetan flower is the vakula and the objects to abandon include delusion.
The Tibetan verse shares the joyful monk and the ending of suffering, without the distinct reference to faith in the Buddha's teaching.
The same Tibetan stanza is also a qualified comparison with Pāli 173. Its opening matches this position more closely, and its image names both sun and moon.
Derge shares the effort to cut the stream and abandon sensuality, with a different second half.
The Tibetan parallel shares meditation, taintlessness, and completing the task, ending instead on the final body.
Two contiguous Tibetan stanzas preserve the day and night images and the radiance of the Buddha.
Tibetan condemns striking or driving away a brahmin. It does not have the Pāli lines on retaliation.
The Tibetan counterpart honors someone who understands Dharma, whether old or young, using the brahmin and fire image.
Derge shares severed tether imagery, with a different list of bonds.
The Tibetan stanza retains attaining the deathless and absence of clinging, while the middle description differs.
The Tibetan stanza retains crossing the flood and letting go of grasping, with differences in the description of the crossing.
Derge retains the exhaustion of craving for becoming and the contrast of this world and the next, without the going-forth clause.
